article_title: Bayesian knowledge tracing, logistic models, and beyond: an overview of learner modeling techniques
citation: Chris Piech, Jonathan Bassen, Jonathan Huang, Surya Ganguli, Mehran Sahami, Leonidas Guibas, Jascha Sohl-Dickstein. (2015). Deep Knowledge Tracing. https://github.com/chrispiech/DeepKnowledgeTracing
title: DKT released code and preprocessed data
description: To facilitate research on deep knowledge tracing, the authors published their model code and preprocessed datasets on GitHub. The article states: "To facilitate research in DKTs we have published our code and relevant preprocessed data" at the repository chrispiech/DeepKnowledgeTracing. This release supports replication of the LSTM/RNN knowledge tracing results and reuse of the training pipeline in follow-up work.
requirements: Requires training data with student interaction sequences and a neural network training setup to reproduce the published results
target_learners: Students on online learning platforms whose interaction data is used for knowledge tracing
target_learning_goals: Predicting student performance on future exercises
examples: The repository accompanies the Assistments, Khan Academy, and simulated-data experiments reported in the paper.
key_sources: Chris Piech, Jonathan Bassen, Jonathan Huang, Surya Ganguli, Mehran Sahami, Leonidas Guibas, Jascha Sohl-Dickstein. (2015). Deep Knowledge Tracing. https://github.com/chrispiech/DeepKnowledgeTracing

article_title: Building dementia knowledge globally through the Understanding Dementia Massive Open Online Course (MOOC)
citation: Eccleston, C., Doherty, K., Bindoff, A., Robinson, A., Vickers, J. & McInerney, F. (2019). Building dementia knowledge globally through the Understanding Dementia Massive Open Online Course (MOOC). npj Science of Learning 4:3. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0042-4
title: Dementia Knowledge Assessment Scale 2.0 (DKAS 2.0)
description: The DKAS 2.0 is a reliable, validated survey used as the pre- and post-course outcome measure in this study. The article states it "comprises 25 items about the characteristics and trajectory of dementia, risk factors and aspects of caring for people with the condition", with items derived from a Delphi study of international experts. Responses are rescored 0–2 and summed to a 0–50 score, enabling objective measurement of knowledge acquisition rather than reliance on engagement or completion metrics.
requirements: Administered before any course content is delivered and again after completing the final unit, with only complete pre-post cases analysed
constraints: Score distribution post-UDMOOC was non-normal, so medians and bootstrap confidence intervals were used
target_learning_goals: Assessing essential dementia knowledge across characteristics, trajectory, risk factors and caring
examples: Used pre and post in the 2016 and 2017 UDMOOC offerings with 4894 complete respondents
key_sources: Eccleston, C., Doherty, K., Bindoff, A., Robinson, A., Vickers, J. & McInerney, F. (2019). Building dementia knowledge globally through the Understanding Dementia Massive Open Online Course (MOOC). npj Science of Learning 4:3. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0042-4

article_title: Development and validation of dysphagia knowledge and self-reported competence questionnaire for nurses.
citation: Mubeen Raffa, Khan Asghar, Kiyani Humaira Shamim, Butt Ayesha Kamal, Bogaardt Hans, Noveen Sadaf. (2026). Development and validation of dysphagia knowledge and self-reported competence questionnaire for nurses. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0358250
title: DKSCQ-N: Dysphagia Knowledge and Self-reported Competence Questionnaire for Nurses
description: The DKSCQ-N is a 21-item questionnaire rated on an 11-point scale (0–10) assessing nurses' dysphagia knowledge and self-reported competence. It covers six domains: anatomy and physiology, risk factors, signs and symptoms, complications, screening and management. The knowledge section uses a graded response format with correct responses and incorrect distractors rated separately, allowing assessment of partial knowledge and misconceptions. Domain scores are converted to percentages for standardisation from 0 to 100.
requirements: Nurses with a minimum of one year of clinical experience working in hospital settings
constraints: Findings may not be fully generalizable to other countries or healthcare systems
Self-reported competence reflects perceived ability and should not be interpreted as directly observed clinical performance
examples: Used with 537 nurses across hospitals in Pakistan for validation
Administered to 46 nurses twice over two weeks for test-retest reliability
key_sources: Mubeen Raffa, Khan Asghar, Kiyani Humaira Shamim, Butt Ayesha Kamal, Bogaardt Hans, Noveen Sadaf. (2026). Development and validation of dysphagia knowledge and self-reported competence questionnaire for nurses. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0358250

article_title: Description of the Dunning-Kruger effect in general surgery residents during laparoscopic cholecystectomy: a blinded prospective study.
citation: Porto Breno Cordeiro, Frati Rodrigo Marcus Cunha, Maltez Rafael Guisalberte, Lima Amanda Ferreira da Silva, Ferreira Tatiane Alves, Baron Larissa Cunha, Passerotti Carlo Camargo, Artifon Everson Luiz, Otoch José Pinhata, da Cruz Jose Arnaldo Shiomi. (2024). Description of the Dunning-Kruger effect in general surgery residents during laparoscopic cholecystectomy: a blinded prospective study. Acta Cirúrgica Brasileira. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11216530/
title: Four competing explanatory accounts of the Dunning-Kruger effect
description: The article reviews four theories offered to explain the Dunning-Kruger effect: metacognitive deficits (low performers lack the skills to recognize their inadequacy), anchoring and adjustment (self-assessments anchor on one's own performance and are inadequately adjusted against others), regression to the mean (a statistical artifact from most people believing they are above average), and motivated reasoning (a self-serving bias maintaining self-esteem). It states the effect's cause "remain multifaceted, ranging from metacognitive shortcomings to statistical phenomena". The article's own data are consistent with the effect but do not adjudicate among these accounts.
requirements: Distinguishing among the accounts requires studies that test the proposed mechanisms, which the article identifies as further work
constraints: The article states the underpinnings of the cause remain multifaceted and unresolved; its own experiment demonstrates existence, not mechanism
examples: The article cites Meeran et al. (2020) as providing evidence for the anchoring-and-adjustment account and Ehrlinger et al. on training reducing the DK effect

(2024). Description of the Dunning-Kruger effect in general surgery residents during laparoscopic cholecystectomy: a blinded prospective study. article_title: The don't know option in progress testing.
citation: Ravesloot C. J., Van der Schaaf M. F., Muijtjens A. M. M., Haaring C., Kruitwagen C. L. J. J., Beek F. J. A., Bakker J., Van Schaik J. P. J., Cate Th. J. Ten. (2015). The don’t know option in progress testing. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-015-9604-2
title: Formula scoring's don't know option as a mechanism linking risk-avoidance tendency to construct-irrelevant score variance
description: The article proposes a mechanism account for why formula scoring distorts knowledge measurement: the DKO score "was considered to be an indicator of the level of risk avoidance of the participant". Risk-taking participants with partial knowledge expect better-than-chance odds and answer, while risk-avoiding participants choose the DKO, so equally knowledgeable participants obtain different FS scores. Because DKO use also declines with knowledge and experience, the mechanism is tested statistically by regressing FS on DKO while controlling for NR score and training length.
requirements: Testing the mechanism requires controlling for knowledge level (NR score) and experience (training length) to isolate the net effect of risk avoidance
constraints: Risk-taking tendency was not measured directly; DKO use at similar knowledge and experience levels served as a proxy, and the account was developed for true/false-item progress tests
target_learning_goals: valid interpretation of progress test scores as knowledge measures
examples: The randomised cross-over study operationalised the mechanism as the additional explained variance of the DKO score in a sequential regression on FS scores
key_sources: Ravesloot C. J., Van der Schaaf M. F., Muijtjens A. M. M., Haaring C., Kruitwagen C. L. J. J., Beek F. J. A., Bakker J., Van Schaik J. P. J., Cate Th. J. Ten. (2015). The don’t know option in progress testing. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-015-9604-2

article_title: The ABCs of DKA: Development and Validation of a Computer-Based Simulator and Scoring System.
citation: Yu Catherine H. Y., Straus Sharon, Brydges Ryan. (2015). The ABCs of DKA: Development and Validation of a Computer-Based Simulator and Scoring System. Journal of General Internal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11606-015-3273-y
title: Computer-based DKA management simulator with six interactive cases and individualized feedback
description: A web-delivered simulator presenting six contrasting DKA clinical scenarios with "interactive order entry, and presentation of laboratory and clinical data". Learning is individualized: if a user fails to administer potassium, the simulated serum potassium falls and targeted feedback appears. Content was built from the Canadian Diabetes Association 2013 guidelines and refined through expert review and heuristic evaluation.
requirements: Expert review of content by clinicians with frequent DKA exposure
Iterative usability refinement over a 12-month development period
constraints: Focuses on DKA management to the exclusion of other medical conditions, which experts noted but authors deemed an acceptable compromise
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning and patient management skills
examples: Six scenarios include DKA with concurrent respiratory alkalosis, hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state in an older adult, and resistant hypokalemia
key_sources: Yu Catherine H. Y., Straus Sharon, Brydges Ryan. (2015). The ABCs of DKA: Development and Validation of a Computer-Based Simulator and Scoring System. Journal of General Internal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11606-015-3273-y

article_title: The ABCs of DKA: Development and Validation of a Computer-Based Simulator and Scoring System.
citation: Yu Catherine H. Y., Straus Sharon, Brydges Ryan. (2015). The ABCs of DKA: Development and Validation of a Computer-Based Simulator and Scoring System. Journal of General Internal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11606-015-3273-y
title: DKA simulator scoring system: seven management domains, 18 performance items, three-point scale yielding scores from 18 to 54
description: The scoring system models the seven priorities of DKA management — potassium deficiency, volume depletion and fluid replacement, acidosis, hyperglycemia, precipitating cause, organization of care, and monitoring of patient — as seven domains comprising "a total of 18 performance items". Each item is scored on a three-point scale (unacceptable, borderline, acceptable), with critical errors identified, producing a final numerical score from 18 to 54.
requirements: Simulator tabulation of percentage of correct actions and identification of critical errors per item
constraints: The exploratory factor analysis was underpowered: the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin value was 0.25, below the recommended 0.50
examples: Critical errors include initiation of insulin when potassium is less than 3.3 and reduction in insulin for blood glucose less than 14.0 mmol/l with persistent elevated anion gap
key_sources: Yu Catherine H. Y., Straus Sharon, Brydges Ryan. (2015). The ABCs of DKA: Development and Validation of a Computer-Based Simulator and Scoring System. Journal of General Internal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11606-015-3273-y
